body_html:
How to think about it

The centre of mass of two masses lies on the line joining them, closer to the heavier one: x = m₂d/(m₁ + m₂). Torque τ = rF sin θ turns a body; moment of inertia I (ring MR², disc ½MR², solid sphere 2/5 MR², rod about its centre ML²/12) resists that turning.

Angular momentum L = Iω is conserved when no external torque acts, so a skater who pulls in her arms spins faster. Rotational kinetic energy is ½Iω². A rolling body has both translational and rotational energy, so a solid sphere rolls down a slope faster than a ring.

Example

1 kg and 3 kg, 4 m apart. CM from 1 kg?

3 × 4 ÷ 4

Answer: 3 m

Example

Disc, M = 2 kg, R = 0.5 m. I?

½ × 2 × 0.25

Answer: 0.25 kg m²

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the centre of mass must be inside the body.
  • Using MR² for every shape.
  • Forgetting sin θ in torque.

faq.q: What is the theorem of parallel axes?
faq.a: I = I<sub>cm</sub> + Md², where d is the distance between the parallel axes.

items.q: Masses of 1 kg and 3 kg are 2 m apart. How far is the centre of mass from the 1 kg mass?
items.e: x = m₂d/(m₁ + m₂) = 3 × 2 ÷ 4 = 1.5 m (closer to the heavier mass).
